subject: biology

items.q: Why does gas exchange become a greater challenge as organisms increase in size?
items.correct: The surface area-to-volume ratio decreases, and the distance from the centre of the organism to its exterior increases.
items.misconception: The surface area-to-volume ratio increases, so far more gas has to cross each unit of the exchange surface.
items.why: Students confuse the total surface area, which does increase with size, with the ratio of surface to volume. In everyday language 'bigger' means 'more of everything', and the idea that one quantity can fall while both of its parts rise is counter-intuitive. The ratio, not the total, is what limits gas exchange. As an organism increases in size its surface area-to-volume ratio decreases, so proportionally less exchange surface is available to supply each unit of respiring volume; this is why large organisms need specialized gas-exchange systems.
items.specStatementText: Gas exchange gets harder as organisms get bigger
items.random_wrong: Only animals with lungs or gills exchange gases, so the challenge arises once an organism is big enough to have them.

items.q: Three cubes are used to model organisms of different sizes. Their surface area-to-volume ratios are: side 1 mm, 6 mm⁻¹; side 2 mm, 3 mm⁻¹; side 4 mm, 1.5 mm⁻¹. Which conclusion is supported by these values?
items.correct: Each doubling of the side halves the ratio, leaving proportionally less surface to supply each unit of volume.
items.misconception: The ratio should have stayed constant as the cubes were scaled up, so the values must contain a measurement error.
items.why: Students apply proportional reasoning from everyday scaling ('twice as big means twice as much of everything') and have not internalized that area scales with the square of length and volume with the cube. Area scales with length squared and volume with length cubed, so volume always grows faster than surface area. Doubling the side of a cube quadruples its surface area but multiplies its volume by eight, halving the ratio; surface area-to-volume ratio therefore decreases with increasing size.
items.specStatementText: Gas exchange gets harder as organisms get bigger
items.random_wrong: The largest cube has the most surface per unit of volume, because its total surface area is the greatest.

items.q: Why is the surface of a gas-exchange organ kept moist?
items.correct: Oxygen and carbon dioxide dissolve in the film of water before diffusing across the cell membranes.
items.misconception: The moisture is not needed for exchange; it only keeps the cells of the surface from drying out and dying.
items.why: Gas exchange is drawn as arrows passing straight from air into blood, and students have not met the idea that a membrane is crossed by molecules in solution. They know that cells die if they dry out, so they attach the moisture to cell survival instead. Gases diffuse across the plasma membranes of the exchange surface only in solution. The thin film of moisture on the surface lets oxygen dissolve before it diffuses into the cells and blood, and carbon dioxide dissolve before it diffuses out; moisture is therefore one of the properties every gas-exchange surface needs, alongside permeability, a thin tissue layer and a large surface area.
items.specStatementText: What a good exchange surface looks like
items.random_wrong: The moisture forms a sticky layer that traps dust and pathogens before they reach the exchange surface.

items.q: A fish rests in still, well-oxygenated water. What keeps the oxygen concentration gradient across its gill surface steep?
items.correct: Water is pumped over the gills while blood flows continuously through their dense capillaries.
items.misconception: The water around the gills contains dissolved oxygen, so the gradient is maintained by the water itself.
items.why: A fish does not visibly breathe in the way a mammal does, and students picture the whole body of water as a uniform reservoir of oxygen rather than as a layer next to the gills that is quickly depleted. Water next to the gill surface loses its oxygen and gains carbon dioxide within moments, and diffusion through still water is very slow. Fish pump water over the gills continuously, ventilating them with water in the same way that mammals ventilate lungs with air, to maintain the concentration gradients.
items.random_wrong: Once oxygen has diffused into the blood the gradient is fixed and does not need to be maintained further.

items.q: Suppose that blood flow through the gill capillaries of an anaesthetized fish is stopped while water continues to flow over the gills, and that oxygen uptake across the gills falls almost to zero within a minute. Which explanation is best supported?
items.correct: With no blood flow, oxygen built up in the stationary blood until its concentration matched the water's, so the gradient was lost.
items.misconception: Stopping blood flow cannot affect the gradient across the gill; the water flowing over the gills must have run out of oxygen.
items.why: Diffusion diagrams show a fixed gradient with one-way arrows and never show the system reaching equilibrium, so students do not appreciate that diffusion itself destroys the gradient that drives it. Diffusion moves substances toward equilibrium, so net movement stops when concentrations equalize. Animals keep the gradient steep by continuously supplying fresh air or water to the exchange surface (ventilation) and by carrying oxygenated blood away and bringing deoxygenated blood in through dense networks of blood vessels.
items.random_wrong: Blood held still in the capillaries should load more fully, so the fall must have been caused by damage to the gill surface.

items.q: What is the function of surfactant in the alveoli of a mammalian lung?
items.correct: It lowers the surface tension of the moisture lining the alveoli, so they do not collapse and inflate easily.
items.misconception: It traps dust and microorganisms in a sticky layer so that they can be swept out of the lungs.
items.why: The only other airway secretion students have met is the mucus of the trachea and bronchi, whose job is trapping particles, so a new secretion in the lungs is assumed to do the same. The word 'surfactant' is unfamiliar and gives no clue. Surfactant is a phospholipid-rich layer on the moist surface of the alveoli. Water has a high surface tension that would tend to pull the walls of each tiny alveolus inward and collapse it; surfactant lowers this surface tension, keeping the alveoli open and making them easy to inflate. Trapping particles is the role of mucus in the airways, not of surfactant.
items.random_wrong: It is the film of water absorbed into the blood, carrying the oxygen dissolved in it across the alveolar wall.

items.q: Mammalian lungs contain a branched network of bronchioles ending in millions of alveoli. How does this branching contribute to gas exchange?
items.correct: It packs a very large alveolar surface, each part close to a capillary bed, into the volume of the thorax.
items.misconception: It multiplies the area of airway wall across which gases are exchanged into the blood as air travels inward.
items.why: Diagrams of the branching airways make the whole tree look like the exchange surface, and students reason that a bigger network of tubes must mean more area for exchange. The branched network of bronchioles is an adaptation for delivering air to millions of alveoli, which is where the thin, moist, capillary-covered exchange surface is. Bronchiole walls are thicker and not in close contact with capillary beds, so they do not exchange gases; the branching increases the exchange area by multiplying the number of alveoli, not by adding airway wall.
items.random_wrong: It lets the lungs grow larger, and a larger organ must have a bigger surface for gas exchange.

items.q: Which sequence of events draws air into the lungs during inspiration?
items.correct: The diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thorax volume rises and lung pressure falls.
items.misconception: Air entering the lungs inflates them, and the inflating lungs push the ribs outward and the diaphragm downward.
items.why: The balloon model of breathing, in which a balloon is blown up and expands its container, reverses the real cause and effect. Students also think of air as actively 'going in' rather than moving passively down a pressure gradient. Air moves only down a pressure gradient. Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles increases the volume of the thorax, which lowers the pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure; air then flows in from outside. The movement of the ribs and diaphragm is the cause, and the inflow of air the consequence.
items.random_wrong: The muscular walls of the lungs contract, widening the alveoli and sucking air in through the trachea.

items.q: A person breathes out as hard as possible. What is the role of the abdominal muscles in this forced expiration?
items.correct: They contract, pushing the abdominal organs up against the relaxed diaphragm so that the volume of the thorax decreases.
items.misconception: They relax so that the diaphragm can rise passively, and so they have no active role in forcing the air out.
items.why: The abdomen visibly moves outward when a person breathes in deeply, so students assume the abdominal muscles are working during inspiration. They also picture the diaphragm being pulled down by something below it rather than contracting itself. The diaphragm moves down by its own contraction, and the abdominal wall bulges because relaxed abdominal muscles let the displaced organs move outward. The abdominal muscles contract only in forced expiration, raising abdominal pressure so the organs push the relaxed diaphragm up into the thorax and reduce its volume.
items.random_wrong: They contract together with the diaphragm, which pushes upward to squeeze the air out of the lungs from below.

items.q: A student's spirometer readings are: tidal volume 0.5 dm³, inspiratory reserve volume 3.0 dm³, expiratory reserve volume 1.2 dm³. What is the student's vital capacity?
items.correct: 4.7 dm³
items.misconception: 4.2 dm³
items.why: The word 'reserve' is read as 'maximum' rather than as 'extra beyond normal'. On a spirometer trace the reserve excursions are large and the tidal breaths small, so students take each big excursion as the reserve measured from the middle. Each reserve volume is measured from the edge of a resting tidal breath, not from its middle: the inspiratory reserve from the top of a normal inhalation to the peak of the deepest inhalation, and the expiratory reserve from the bottom of a normal exhalation to the end of the deepest exhalation. Vital capacity is therefore tidal volume plus both reserves.
items.random_wrong: 3.5 dm³

items.q: Which statement correctly defines vital capacity?
items.correct: The maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after the deepest possible inhalation.
items.misconception: The maximum volume that can be inhaled in one breath from the end of a normal exhalation.
items.why: The word 'capacity' suggests filling up from where you are, so students picture a maximal inhalation starting from a normal breath and forget that the expiratory reserve, the air that can additionally be forced out, is part of what can be exhaled. Vital capacity is measured from the peak of a maximal inhalation to the end of a maximal exhalation. It includes the expiratory reserve volume below a resting breath as well as the tidal volume and the inspiratory reserve volume above it.
items.random_wrong: The maximum volume that can be exhaled after a normal, resting inhalation.

items.q: Which adaptation of a leaf allows carbon dioxide to reach the photosynthesizing cells inside it?
items.correct: Air spaces between the spongy mesophyll cells connect to the stomata, so the gas diffuses to every cell.
items.misconception: The cuticle and epidermis are permeable to gases, so carbon dioxide diffuses in across the whole surface of the leaf.
items.why: Leaves are taught as being thin and flat to give a large surface area for diffusion, so students assume the whole surface is the exchange surface, as it is in a unicellular organism. The waxy cuticle is impermeable and the epidermal cells are tightly packed, so almost no gas crosses the leaf surface directly. Gases enter and leave through the stomata, and the large thin shape of the leaf matters because it brings every mesophyll cell close to an air space fed by stomata.
items.specStatementText: How a leaf is adapted for gas exchange
items.random_wrong: The veins carry carbon dioxide into the leaf from the stem and roots and take the oxygen produced away.

items.q: What causes a stoma to open?
items.correct: The guard cells take up water and swell, and their unevenly thickened walls make them bend apart.
items.misconception: The guard cells contract like muscle cells, pulling the two edges of the pore apart from one another.
items.why: Opening and closing are associated with muscles, and the guard cells are the only cells shown moving, so students supply a contraction mechanism. Plant cells changing shape by turgor is unfamiliar. Plant cells have no contractile machinery; guard cells change shape by changes in turgor. When they gain water they swell and, because the wall next to the pore is thicker than the outer wall, they bow apart and the stoma opens; when they lose water they become flaccid and the stoma closes.
items.specStatementText: How a leaf is adapted for gas exchange
items.random_wrong: The guard cells lose water and shrink, leaving a gap between them through which the gases can pass.

items.q: Which statement about a plan diagram of a transverse section of a dicotyledonous leaf is correct?
items.correct: It shows the outline and position of each tissue, with the palisade mesophyll directly beneath the upper epidermis.
items.misconception: It shows a few representative cells of each tissue in outline, including their nuclei and chloroplasts.
items.why: Every earlier drawing students have made under a microscope has been of cells, so 'drawing the leaf' is assumed to mean drawing its cells. The distinction between a low-power plan and a high-power detail drawing is new. A plan diagram is drawn at low power to show the distribution of tissues: the upper and lower epidermis, the palisade and spongy mesophyll, and the veins with their xylem and phloem, each shown as a labelled region bounded by lines. Individual cells are shown only in a high-power drawing of a small part of the section.
items.random_wrong: It shows each vein with phloem above the xylem, because the phloem lies nearer to the upper surface.

items.q: Why is transpiration described as a consequence of gas exchange rather than as a process the leaf carries out for its own sake?
items.correct: Stomata must be open for carbon dioxide to enter, and water vapour inevitably diffuses out through the same pores.
items.misconception: The plant opens its stomata in order to lose water, because transpiration is needed to pull water up through the xylem.
items.why: Earlier courses present the 'transpiration stream' as the plant's water-transport system, so students treat water loss as the purpose of the stomata. Any effect that is useful gets reinterpreted as an intention. Stomata open to admit carbon dioxide, and water loss follows unavoidably because the air spaces inside the leaf are saturated with water vapour and the atmosphere usually is not. The plant regulates stomatal opening to limit this loss, closing stomata when water is short even at the cost of photosynthesis; the pull that transpiration exerts on the xylem is a consequence, not the reason stomata open.
items.random_wrong: Water vapour escapes across the cuticle and epidermis wherever gases are exchanged over the leaf surface.

items.q: A potometer was used to estimate transpiration by a leafy shoot at 20 °C. Water uptake in still air was 0.8 cm³ per hour; with a fan blowing air across the leaves, 1.9 cm³ per hour; in still air with a clear plastic bag enclosing the shoot, 0.3 cm³ per hour. Which conclusion is supported by these results?
items.correct: Moving air and low humidity both steepen the water-vapour gradient from the air spaces to the atmosphere.
items.misconception: Moving air raised the rate because the fan warmed the leaves, and warmer leaves evaporate water faster.
items.why: Students know wind chill and hair dryers, so they attribute any effect of moving air to temperature. The layer of still, humid air that builds up at a leaf surface is invisible and not intuitive. In still air, water vapour leaving the stomata accumulates around the leaf and reduces the gradient. Wind sweeps this humid layer away and replaces it with drier air, steepening the gradient and increasing transpiration, independently of any change in temperature.
items.random_wrong: The humid air inside the bag should have increased the rate, so the reading of 0.3 cm³ per hour must be a fault.

items.q: A student counts the stomata visible in five different fields of view on the lower epidermis of a leaf: 22, 26, 19, 27 and 21. The area of one field of view at high power is 0.20 mm². What is the stomatal density?
items.correct: 115 per mm²
items.misconception: 575 per mm²
items.why: Students pool their replicate counts as if they were one big sample, and forget that the pooled count came from several fields, so the area must be scaled up in the same way or the counts averaged first. Density is a count per unit area. Either average the counts and divide the mean by the area of one field, or divide the total count by the total area counted; both give the same result. Dividing the total count by the area of a single field overestimates the density by a factor equal to the number of fields.
items.random_wrong: 110 per mm²

items.q: Three students estimated the stomatal density of leaves from the same plant. Student A counted one field of view at high power and reported 90 per mm². Student B counted ten different fields, obtained values between 60 and 130 per mm², and reported the mean, 95 per mm². Student C counted the same single field as A five times, getting 90 per mm² each time. Which evaluation of these results is best?
items.correct: B's estimate is most reliable, because the spread shows the leaf varies and the mean averages it out.
items.misconception: C's result is the most reliable, because repeating the count five times confirmed that no counting error had been made.
items.why: Earlier courses present repetition as a way to spot anomalous results or errors, so students think a single count is fine provided it was done carefully. They also expect a leaf to be uniform. Biological material is variable: the number of stomata in different fields of view on the same leaf genuinely differs. Repeated counts illustrate this variability, and the mean of replicate counts is a more reliable estimate of the density than any single count, however carefully made.
items.random_wrong: B's method is the least reliable, because results that vary from 60 to 130 show that the counting was inconsistent.

items.q: What is meant by cooperative binding of oxygen to haemoglobin?
items.correct: Binding of oxygen to one haem group changes the conformation of the protein so the remaining haem groups bind oxygen more readily.
items.misconception: Each of the four haem groups binds oxygen independently, with the same affinity whether or not the others are occupied.
items.why: Haemoglobin is introduced as a molecule that 'carries four oxygens', and students picture four separate sockets. Cooperative effects between parts of one protein are a new idea. Haemoglobin's four subunits interact. The first oxygen binds with difficulty; once bound it shifts the shape of the whole molecule so that the second, third and fourth bind progressively more easily. This cooperative binding is why the oxygen dissociation curve is S-shaped rather than a simple saturating curve.
items.random_wrong: Oxygen and carbon dioxide share the haem groups, taking turns to bind as their concentrations change in the blood.

items.q: In the placenta, maternal blood and foetal blood are separated by a thin barrier. How is oxygen transferred from maternal blood to foetal blood?
items.correct: Foetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen, so at the oxygen concentration in the placenta it loads oxygen that maternal haemoglobin releases.
items.misconception: Foetal haemoglobin has a lower affinity for oxygen, so that it releases oxygen to the rapidly growing foetal tissues more easily than adult haemoglobin would.
items.why: Students focus on unloading and reason that a growing foetus needs oxygen delivered quickly. They do not consider that the foetus must first take oxygen from maternal blood that is already releasing it, which requires a higher affinity. Foetal haemoglobin has different polypeptide subunits and a higher affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin, so its dissociation curve lies to the left. In the placenta both haemoglobins experience the same oxygen concentration; because the foetal form binds more strongly, oxygen released by maternal haemoglobin is taken up by foetal haemoglobin.
items.random_wrong: Maternal red blood cells pass across the barrier into the foetal circulation and deliver their oxygen directly to the foetus.

items.q: During vigorous exercise a muscle produces large amounts of carbon dioxide. How does this affect the delivery of oxygen to the muscle?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide lowers haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so more oxygen dissociates at the oxygen concentration in the muscle.
items.misconception: Haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen rises in the working muscle so that it can hold on to more oxygen for delivery to the muscle cells.
items.why: Students equate 'affinity' with 'ability to deliver', reasoning that more need should mean more affinity. The word affinity suggests attraction, and attraction sounds helpful. High affinity means haemoglobin holds on to oxygen, which is what is wanted in the lungs, not in a working muscle. In respiring tissue carbon dioxide lowers the affinity (the Bohr shift), so a larger fraction of the oxygen carried is released exactly where it is needed.
items.random_wrong: Only the low oxygen concentration in the working muscle causes extra unloading; carbon dioxide itself has no effect on haemoglobin.

items.q: Adult haemoglobin is about 20% saturated with oxygen at a partial pressure of oxygen of 2 kPa, 60% at 4 kPa, 90% at 8 kPa and 98% at 13 kPa. Which explanation accounts for this pattern?
items.correct: Saturation rises steeply from 2 to 8 kPa because each oxygen bound raises the affinity of the other haem groups.
items.misconception: The curve shows the order in which haemoglobin loads over time, from its arrival in the lungs to full saturation.
items.why: Most graphs students meet have time on the x-axis, and the story of blood loading in the lungs and unloading in tissues is told as a journey, so the curve is read as that journey from left to right. The curve is a plot of percentage saturation against oxygen concentration. Any point on it gives the saturation that haemoglobin reaches at that oxygen concentration; the lungs and the tissues correspond to different positions along the x-axis because their oxygen concentrations differ, not to different times.
items.random_wrong: The four haem groups fill one after another at equal rates, so saturation rises in direct proportion to the oxygen concentration.

items.q: Two oxygen dissociation curves are compared. Curve X lies to the left of curve Y: at a partial pressure of oxygen of 4 kPa, haemoglobin X is 75% saturated and haemoglobin Y is 60% saturated. What can be concluded?
items.correct: Haemoglobin X has the higher affinity for oxygen, because it is more fully loaded at the same oxygen concentration as Y.
items.misconception: Haemoglobin X has the lower affinity for oxygen, because its curve lies further to the left on the axis.
items.why: Students read 'left = less' from the x-axis and transfer it to affinity, instead of comparing the two curves at the same oxygen concentration. Compare the curves at one oxygen concentration: the left-hand curve is higher, so that haemoglobin is more saturated at the same concentration and has the higher affinity. Foetal haemoglobin's curve lies to the left of the adult curve; the Bohr shift moves a curve to the right, lowering affinity.
items.random_wrong: Haemoglobin X loaded before Y, because the curve further to the left represents an earlier time.

items.q: Do organisms without lungs or gills, such as unicellular organisms, carry out gas exchange?
items.correct: Yes. Gas exchange is a vital function in all organisms; a unicellular organism exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide by diffusion across its plasma membrane.
items.misconception: Gas exchange is the same thing as breathing, so only animals with lungs or gills exchange gases.
items.why: In everyday language 'breathing' covers the whole process of obtaining oxygen, and lungs are the only gas-exchange structure most students have seen, so gas exchange is equated with the visible act of ventilating lungs. Gas exchange is the diffusion of gases across a surface, and it takes place in every organism, including unicellular organisms, plants and fungi. Ventilation (breathing) is a separate process, found only in some animals, that maintains concentration gradients at the exchange surface.
items.specStatementText: Gas exchange gets harder as organisms get bigger
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is diffusion alone not sufficient to supply oxygen to the cells at the centre of a large animal?
items.correct: Because the distance from the exterior to the centre is large, and the time diffusion takes rises steeply with distance, so oxygen would arrive far too slowly.
items.misconception: Diffusion distance does not matter: gases diffuse quickly through tissue regardless of how far they have to travel, so only the size of the surface limits gas exchange.
items.why: Classroom demonstrations of diffusion (a smell spreading across a room, a dye spreading in water) make diffusion look fast over metres, and diagrams show diffusion as simple arrows with no sense of time or distance. Diffusion is only rapid over microscopic distances; over millimetres it takes minutes and over centimetres far longer. As organisms increase in size the distance from the centre to the exterior increases, which is one of the two reasons gas exchange becomes more challenging, alongside the fall in surface area-to-volume ratio.
items.specStatementText: Gas exchange gets harder as organisms get bigger
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does a gas-exchange organ achieve a large surface area?
items.correct: By subdividing or folding its surface many times, as in the millions of alveoli of a lung or the filaments and lamellae of a gill, so that a large area is packed into a small volume.
items.misconception: A large surface area for gas exchange is achieved by making the organ larger, so a bigger lung has more area simply because it is bigger.
items.why: Students equate size with area. They have not yet separated the outer size of an organ from the internal area produced by folding and subdividing, and lungs are drawn from the outside as simple bags. Enlarging an organ increases its volume faster than its surface, which is exactly the problem. Exchange surfaces get their large area from internal subdivision: the alveoli of a pair of human lungs have a combined surface area of tens of square metres within a chest cavity of a few litres.
items.specStatementText: What a good exchange surface looks like
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does oxygen enter the blood dissolved in water that is absorbed across the exchange surface?
items.correct: No. Oxygen dissolves in the moisture on the surface and then diffuses on its own across the membranes into the blood; the water itself is not absorbed.
items.misconception: Oxygen is carried into the blood by water: the moisture on the exchange surface is absorbed, taking the dissolved oxygen with it.
items.why: Students learn that gases dissolve in the moist surface and that fish take oxygen from water, and they run the two ideas together into a picture of oxygen being 'drunk' in with water. Absorption of dissolved substances with water is also how they picture the gut. The moisture on an exchange surface is a stationary film in which gases dissolve; the dissolved oxygen then diffuses down its concentration gradient across the plasma membranes into the blood. Water is not taken up with it, and the film has to be replenished only because some evaporates.
items.specStatementText: What a good exchange surface looks like
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Would blood load more oxygen if it stayed longer in the capillaries of an exchange surface?
items.correct: No. Continuous flow is what keeps the gradient steep: blood that lingers approaches equilibrium with the outside and net diffusion stops, whereas blood that keeps moving is replaced by deoxygenated blood that can go on loading.
items.misconception: Blood should be held still or slowed in the capillaries of the exchange surface so that it has time to fill up with oxygen.
items.why: An intuitive 'soaking' model: things absorb more the longer they are left. Students have not linked the rate of diffusion to the gradient, which is lost as blood approaches equilibrium. Diffusion across an exchange surface depends on the concentration gradient, and blood reaches equilibrium with the air or water outside within a fraction of a second in the capillaries. Continuous blood flow removes the oxygenated blood and replaces it with deoxygenated blood, so the gradient, and therefore diffusion, is maintained.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the lungs contract and expand by themselves to move air?
items.correct: No. Lungs contain no skeletal muscle; they are inflated and deflated by pressure changes created when the diaphragm, intercostal muscles and abdominal muscles change the volume of the thorax.
items.misconception: The lungs are muscular organs that inflate and deflate themselves, sucking air in and squeezing it out.
items.why: In everyday speech the lungs 'breathe', and the visible expansion of the chest is attributed to the lungs themselves; models of lungs as balloons that are blown up reinforce the idea that the lung is the active part. The lungs are passive, elastic organs. Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles increases the volume of the thorax, lowering the pressure inside the lungs so air flows in; relaxation of these muscles, helped in forced expiration by the internal intercostal and abdominal muscles, decreases the volume and forces air out.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does the diaphragm do during inspiration and during expiration?
items.correct: During inspiration it contracts and flattens, increasing the volume of the thorax; during expiration it relaxes and returns to a dome shape, which decreases the volume.
items.misconception: The diaphragm contracts and pushes upward to force air out during expiration, and relaxes to let air in during inspiration.
items.why: Diagrams show the diaphragm as an upward dome, so students picture its 'active' state as pushing up. They also associate contraction with squeezing something out and relaxation with letting something in. A muscle can only pull, not push: when the diaphragm contracts it flattens and moves down, enlarging the thorax for inspiration. Expiration happens when it relaxes and the abdominal organs, pushed by the abdominal muscles in forced expiration, return it to its dome shape.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is vital capacity measured?
items.correct: The subject inhales as deeply as possible and then exhales as fully as possible into the spirometer; the volume exhaled is the vital capacity.
items.misconception: Vital capacity is the maximum volume that can be exhaled after a normal breath in, so it is the tidal volume plus the expiratory reserve volume.
items.why: Vital capacity is measured by blowing out into a bag, tube or spirometer, so students focus on the exhalation and forget that it must be preceded by a maximal inhalation; they measure the exhalation from wherever their breathing happens to be. Vital capacity requires a maximal inhalation first. The volume then exhaled runs from the peak of inspiration to the end of a forced expiration, and equals tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve plus expiratory reserve. Exhaling fully after only a normal breath measures a smaller volume.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is vital capacity the same as the total volume of air the lungs can hold?
items.correct: No. Some air always remains in the lungs even after the deepest possible exhalation, so the total lung volume is larger than the vital capacity.
items.misconception: Vital capacity is the total volume of air in the lungs when they are completely full.
items.why: 'Capacity' in everyday use means how much a container holds, and students assume the lungs can be emptied completely, like a balloon, so the volume breathed out must equal the volume the lungs contain. Vital capacity is the maximum volume that can be exhaled after a maximal inhalation. The lungs cannot be fully emptied by exhaling, because the alveoli and airways retain air, so the vital capacity measured with a spirometer is less than the total volume of the lungs.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which tissue provides the gas-exchange surface of a leaf, and what are the air spaces for?
items.correct: The moist surfaces of the mesophyll cells bordering the air spaces, mainly in the spongy mesophyll; the interconnected air spaces let gases diffuse from the stomata to every cell, including the palisade cells.
items.misconception: The palisade mesophyll is the gas-exchange surface, because it does most of the photosynthesis, and the air spaces in the spongy mesophyll are just storage spaces or gaps.
items.why: Attention in photosynthesis lessons goes to the chloroplast-rich palisade cells, so students assume those cells must also be where gases are exchanged, and treat the loosely packed spongy layer as unimportant packing. Gas exchange happens where a moist cell surface meets air, and that is mainly in the spongy mesophyll, whose loosely packed cells border a network of air spaces opening to the stomata. The air spaces are the route by which carbon dioxide reaches the palisade cells above and oxygen leaves them; they give the leaf a large internal surface area for exchange.

items.q: What do the veins of a leaf transport?
items.correct: Water and dissolved mineral ions into the leaf in the xylem, and sugars out of the leaf in the phloem; gases are not transported by veins.
items.misconception: Leaf veins carry carbon dioxide into the leaf and oxygen out of it, like blood vessels carrying gases in an animal.
items.why: Students transfer the animal model, in which blood vessels carry oxygen and carbon dioxide, to the plant. Both systems are called 'transport systems' and drawn as branching networks. Gases move through a leaf only by diffusion, entering and leaving through the stomata and moving through the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll. The veins' xylem supplies water, which replaces the water lost in transpiration and keeps the mesophyll surfaces moist so that gases can dissolve; their phloem removes the sugars made in photosynthesis.

items.q: Does a stoma open when its guard cells shrink?
items.correct: No. A stoma opens when the guard cells swell with water; the swelling bends them apart because their walls are unevenly thickened. Shrinking (loss of turgor) closes the pore.
items.misconception: Guard cells open the stoma by losing water and shrinking, leaving a gap between them, and close it by swelling up to fill the gap.
items.why: Intuitively, smaller cells should leave a bigger hole and swollen cells should block it. Students have not seen that the uneven thickening of the guard cell walls makes swelling bend the cells outward. Guard cells have a thick inner wall next to the pore and a thinner outer wall. When they take up water and become turgid, the thin outer wall stretches more, so each cell curves away from its partner and the pore opens. When they lose water, they straighten and the pore closes.

items.q: In a vein of a dicotyledonous leaf, which lies nearer the upper surface, xylem or phloem?
items.correct: The xylem; the phloem lies below it, toward the lower epidermis.
items.misconception: The phloem lies above the xylem in a leaf vein, nearer the upper surface.
items.why: Students transfer the arrangement of a stem, where phloem lies outside the xylem, and treat 'outside' as 'upper'. The two tissues are also often drawn side by side with no indication of orientation. In a transverse section of a dicotyledonous leaf, each vein has xylem toward the upper (adaxial) surface and phloem toward the lower (abaxial) surface, and a plan diagram should show them in that order.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which mesophyll layer lies directly beneath the upper epidermis of a dicotyledonous leaf?
items.correct: The palisade mesophyll; the spongy mesophyll lies below it, above the lower epidermis.
items.misconception: The spongy mesophyll lies just under the upper epidermis, with the palisade layer beneath it near the lower surface.
items.why: The layer names are learnt as a list without a spatial picture, and students reason that the chloroplast-rich palisade cells would be safer 'deep inside' the leaf rather than exposed at the top. From the upper surface downward the tissues are upper epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll and lower epidermis. The palisade cells sit directly under the transparent upper epidermis because that is where light enters, and the spongy layer with its air spaces sits above the lower epidermis, where most stomata are.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does high humidity affect the rate of transpiration?
items.correct: It decreases the rate, because the concentration gradient of water vapour between the air spaces of the leaf and the atmosphere is smaller.
items.misconception: High humidity increases transpiration, because there is more water around and the leaf is wetter.
items.why: In everyday language 'humid' means 'wet', and students reason that more water means more water movement. They have not connected transpiration to a diffusion gradient of water vapour. Water vapour diffuses out of a leaf down its concentration gradient, from the saturated air spaces to the drier air outside. In humid air the gradient is small, so the rate of transpiration falls; in dry air it is large, so the rate rises.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does light intensity affect the rate of transpiration?
items.correct: Yes. In the light the stomata open, so water vapour can diffuse out; in darkness they close and transpiration falls to a low level.
items.misconception: Transpiration is just evaporation from the leaf surface, controlled by temperature, and it goes on at the same rate whether or not the stomata are open or the light is on.
items.why: Evaporation from puddles and washing lines depends on temperature and wind, and students apply this everyday model to the leaf, forgetting that the water evaporates inside the leaf and can only escape through stomata. Most water leaves a leaf through the stomata, so anything that changes stomatal opening changes the rate. Light causes stomata to open, so transpiration is higher in the light than in the dark at the same temperature; the waxy cuticle keeps direct evaporation from the surface small.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: The area of the field of view is known. How is the count converted to a density?
items.correct: Divide the count by the area of the field of view, giving stomata per mm².
items.misconception: To convert a count to a density you multiply the count by the area of the field of view.
items.why: Students know the area must be 'used' but read 'per' as a scaling-up operation, and multiplying is what scaling up usually means. The result, a few stomata per mm², does not look obviously wrong to them. Density means number per unit area, so the count is divided by the area in which it was made. A count of 23 in a field of 0.20 mm² gives 23 ÷ 0.20 = 115 stomata per mm²; multiplying would give 4.6, a value far below any real leaf.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Repeated counts of stomata in different fields of view give different numbers. Does this show the technique is faulty?
items.correct: No. It shows the natural variability of biological material; replicate counts are taken precisely so that this variability can be averaged out.
items.misconception: If replicate counts differ from one another, the counting was inconsistent and the results are unreliable, so the method has failed.
items.why: Students expect a good experiment to give identical repeats, as physical measurements often nearly do, and read any scatter as human error rather than as a property of the material. Living material varies, so replicate counts are expected to differ. Their spread is information about the variability of the leaf, and the mean of many replicates is more reliable than any single count; this is the reason for replicate trials, not evidence against them.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Would counting one larger field of view at low power be as reliable as counting several fields at high power?
items.correct: No. Stomata are hard to see and count accurately at low power, and one field, however large, samples only one region of the leaf; several separate high-power fields sample its variability.
items.misconception: Reliability comes from counting more stomata, so a single large field of view at low power is better than several small fields at high power.
items.why: 'Bigger sample is better' is applied to the size of one field instead of to the number of independent replicates, and students overlook that individual stomata cannot be resolved reliably at low power. Stomatal density is counted in the field of view at high power, where each stoma can be identified. Reliability is then increased by repeating the count in several different fields of view, which samples the variation across the leaf, rather than by enlarging one field.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does carbon dioxide bind to haemoglobin?
items.correct: At sites on the polypeptide chains away from the haem groups: this is allosteric binding, and it changes the protein's conformation so that its affinity for oxygen falls.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide binds to the same haem groups as oxygen and competes with it, displacing oxygen from the molecule.
items.why: Students know that carbon monoxide competes with oxygen for the haem groups, and generalize to carbon dioxide. The everyday picture of red blood cells 'swapping' oxygen for carbon dioxide also suggests exchange at one site. Carbon dioxide does not bind to the iron of the haem group. It binds allosterically, to amino groups on the globin chains, and this binding alters the shape of the protein so that oxygen is released more readily. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are therefore not competing for the same site; carbon dioxide acts by lowering haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Between what does the cooperation in 'cooperative binding' occur?
items.correct: Between the four haem groups (subunits) within a single haemoglobin molecule; binding of oxygen at one raises the affinity of the others.
items.misconception: Cooperative binding means haemoglobin molecules cooperate with each other, joining together or helping one another to carry oxygen in clusters.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'cooperate' is between separate individuals, so students look for cooperation between molecules rather than within one. They have not yet met the idea of conformational change spreading through a single protein. Cooperative binding is a property of one molecule. Haemoglobin has four subunits, each with a haem group, and oxygen binding at one subunit changes the conformation of the whole protein so the remaining haem groups bind oxygen more readily. Separate haemoglobin molecules do not interact.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does oxygen pass from the mother to the foetus in the placenta?
items.correct: By diffusion from maternal blood to foetal blood across the placental tissues; the two circulations do not mix, and foetal haemoglobin's higher affinity lets it take up the oxygen that maternal haemoglobin releases.
items.misconception: Maternal blood, or maternal red blood cells, cross into the foetal circulation and deliver oxygen directly.
items.why: Everyday language about a mother 'sharing her blood' with the baby, and diagrams that show the placenta as a single blood-filled space, suggest that the two blood supplies are connected. Maternal and foetal blood are separated by the placental barrier and never mix. Oxygen diffuses across this barrier down its concentration gradient, and the transfer is made efficient by foetal haemoglobin, which has a higher affinity for oxygen than the adult form and so loads oxygen at the oxygen concentration at which maternal haemoglobin unloads it.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is more oxygen released from haemoglobin in a rapidly respiring tissue than in a resting one?
items.correct: Partly because the oxygen concentration is lower, but also because the higher carbon dioxide concentration lowers haemoglobin's affinity, so at any given oxygen concentration more oxygen dissociates.
items.misconception: Extra oxygen is released in respiring tissue only because the tissue has used up oxygen and its concentration is low; carbon dioxide has no effect on haemoglobin itself.
items.why: Students have a working model of diffusion down a concentration gradient and apply it alone, without any idea that the carrier protein's properties can change with conditions. The Bohr shift means the dissociation curve moves to the right when carbon dioxide concentration rises. So at the same oxygen concentration haemoglobin is less saturated in a tissue producing much carbon dioxide than in one producing little: the extra unloading is due to the effect of carbon dioxide on haemoglobin, not just to the lower oxygen concentration.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a high percentage saturation on the dissociation curve mean that a lot of oxygen is being delivered to the tissues?
items.correct: No. Saturation is how much oxygen haemoglobin is holding. Oxygen is delivered where saturation falls, in the steep region of the curve at the oxygen concentrations found in respiring tissues.
items.misconception: The percentage saturation on the curve is the amount of oxygen being given to the tissues, so the plateau at high oxygen concentration is where haemoglobin unloads most oxygen.
items.why: The y-axis is read as 'oxygen' in general rather than as oxygen bound to haemoglobin, and the plateau, being the top of the graph, is taken as the region of greatest activity. The plateau corresponds to the lungs, where haemoglobin loads to near-full saturation and small changes in oxygen concentration make little difference. The steep part of the curve corresponds to respiring tissues: there a small fall in oxygen concentration produces a large fall in saturation, which is the oxygen released to the tissue.
